_meta.model: claude-sonnet-4-6 (MODELS.SMART), 1 endpoint (/signal-vs-noise, fans out to 2 parallel calls merged server-side)
_meta.baseline_commit: signalvsnoise-v8 (owner-supplied researched rebuild: web-search pre-pass + cited synthesis)
_meta.v5_note: v4's regex (CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE) was verb-conjugation-specific ('evidence shows/suggests/supports') and missed 12 of 13 real violations in the very next live test, a parenting/screen-time topic: 'the evidence tends to show,' 'observational research,' 'reviews of homework research... broadly recognized in ... literature,' 'researchers argue,' 'is associated with,' 'historically,' 'documented,' 'the evidence on X is Y.' Narrow verb-matching does not generalize across the many ways a model phrases 'I reviewed a body of evidence' — v5's list is now broad WORD/PHRASE matching (evidence/research + up to 3 words + a wide verb set, bare 'literature'/'historically'/'documented'/'associated with', etc.), verified against all 13 new violations plus 7 legitimate ALLOWED sentences (0 false positives, 0 false negatives) before shipping. ARCHITECTURE CHANGE: enforcement moved from a whole-CALL regenerate (v4) to PER-FIELD regenerate (v5) — enforceClaimModeFields()/regenerateField()/setAtPath() rewrite only the flagged sentence (cheap, MODELS.FAST, no JSON schema to fill), preserving everything the model got right instead of risking a whole-half regenerate trading one violation for a different one elsewhere. A field that still fails after its one regeneration attempt is left as-is and the EXISTING structural clean()-filter (unchanged) drops the enclosing item, same fallback as before. NEW: a traceability/scope-creep guard (rule 21 extended + 5 new outputGuard entries) — the same live test also introduced 'free-range parenting' and invented 'the core of free-range parenting' as a model-generated definition, neither of which the visitor raised (visitor supplied only screen time, tiger vs. free-range as a *label pair*, and homework — not a definition of any of them). Rule 21 now states an explicit traceability test (A: a supplied claim, B: a necessary distinction, C: an examined source — if none apply, don't write it). Also reinforced: rule 26 (new) — the_signal doesn't need one item per noise item, don't insert an unprompted epistemic lesson (e.g. 'before-and-after comparisons') the visitor didn't raise, don't invent an individual child/person to apply a population claim to (that belongs in what_general_claims_cant_decide, not the general bottom line). UI: a 'CLAIM ANALYSIS' mode badge with a tooltip now renders under ANALYZING (source_analysis/verified_research labels are unreachable today — this tool performs no live retrieval — and are not yet built; add them only if that capability is ever added). Catalog copy (src/data/tools.js description/seoDescription/primer.get) and svn_tagline reworded away from 'stronger evidence'/'genuinely unsettled' framing that implied the tool always has access to an evidence base, per the same principle as SOURCE MODE. Live-tested against the exact parenting/screen-time/homework scenario (0 banned-phrase hits, 0 field-fix regenerations needed — the strengthened prompt got it right without needing the backstop this time; the backstop's correctness was verified separately via 20 unit test cases against the regex directly). DO NOT revert to whole-call regeneration or narrow the banned-phrase list back to verb-conjugation matching — both were the specific gaps this pass closed.
_meta.v4_note: A THIRD 'final corrections' pass, same day as v3, found the identical literature-review-voice failure in a domain not yet tested — finance ('persistent tracking of fund returns... across multiple markets and asset classes,' 'the evidence covers funds that survived long enough to be measured,' a fabricated survivorship-bias limitation for a dataset never examined). Three prompt-only passes had not fully suppressed this, so v4 adds what they didn't have: a deterministic, ENGLISH-ONLY code-level backstop (see signal-vs-noise.js's CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE / findBannedPhrase / callClaimModeChecked) — every prose field is scanned against a fixed phrase list, a violating half is regenerated once with the exact offending phrase quoted back at it, and any array item that still violates after that is silently dropped rather than shown. The prompt still tries hard to get it right the first time (extensive new PERSONALITY rules, worked BAD/GOOD examples for the fee/valuation/real-estate/survivorship/professional-referral/ranking-against-unnamed-alternatives failures) — the regex is the guarantee, not a replacement for it. SCHEMA CHANGE: genuinely_debated (with nullable what_supports_one_view/another_view, introduced in v3) is REMOVED entirely and replaced by two separate top-level arrays: still_worth_verifying[] ({question, why_it_matters, what_would_help} — a genuinely unresolved GENERAL empirical question, never a fabricated two-sided debate) and what_general_claims_cant_decide[] (plain strings — person-specific questions a general analysis can never resolve, e.g. 'whether direct real estate fits your actual situation'). v3's null-views mechanism for person-dependent questions is superseded by this split, not extended. Response also gains analysis_mode ('claim_analysis', hard-locked in code, not model-self-reported) and sources_examined (always [] today — no source-paste feature exists). Caps changed: the_signal 4->3, still_worth_verifying capped at 2 (was genuinely_debated at 3), what_general_claims_cant_decide capped at 3, the_bottom_line.what_would_change_the_answer 2->3. i18n: svn_nuance reworded 'Limits:' -> "What it doesn't establish:"; svn_debated_header reworded 'Still Unsettled' -> 'Still Worth Verifying'; new keys svn_verify_why/svn_verify_would_help/svn_cant_decide_header; svn_one_view/svn_another_view/svn_why_unsettled are now orphaned (left in the locale files, no longer referenced in JSX — the two-sided-debate UI was removed, not relabeled). outputGuard.prohibit grew from 28 to 37 entries. DO NOT reverse the schema split or the code-level regex backstop — three prompt-only passes already proved insufficient on their own.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden signal-vs-noise). v2 (2026-09-09) fixed the health-domain instances of the tool implying a literature review it never performed. v3 (2026-09-10) fixed the SAME failure mode recurring in a non-health (career/labor) domain — 'wage data shows,' an invented MBA-recruiting market map, an invented causal mechanism for job-switching pay, a strawmanned 'follow your passion' critique, an extra unrequested career-advice claim, two noise_type mislabels, an unsupported publicity/selection-bias claim used to rebut an overclaim with another overclaim, debate-club phrasing, and a STILL UNSETTLED section forced into a two-sided-evidence shape it didn't have for a person-dependent question. v4 (same day) is documented in v4_note above. v5 (2026-09-10) is documented in v5_note above. v6 (2026-09-10) is documented in v6_note above.
_meta.prior_notes: v2 (2026-09-09) was a full owner-supplied rewrite: the v1 tool asserted "real consensus," named specific actors as "generating noise," and invoked specific research designs, biomarkers, genetic variants, and validation findings from memory as though it had performed a sourced evidence review — exactly the authority the tool was never in a position to claim. Schema changed completely from v1 (why_this_field_is_noisy -> framing; the_signal.items[].why_we_know_this -> basis; .the_nuance -> limits; genuinely_debated[].side_a/side_b -> what_supports_one_view/what_supports_another_view (later removed entirely in v4); the_noise[] gained what_the_evidence_supports_instead alongside renamed what_went_wrong (was the_problem); the_bottom_line's three single-string fields became three arrays; sources_of_noise[].actor/incentive/how_to_spot_it -> source_type/how_it_distorts/how_to_recognize_it, no longer naming an accused actor). Guards added that pass: NO_QUOTE_RULE, router.outputStandard='v2' + outputGuard, and a post-guard structural validation pass (see code comment: the guard mutates its argument in place and its repair pass can leave a field incomplete despite instructions not to).
_meta.v6_note: A FOURTH 'final corrections' pass, sleep domain, confirmed the deterministic claim_analysis mode switch (v4) had finally killed the fake-literature-review voice, but found a narrower, different failure: unlabeled empirical premises imported from memory that never use evidence-provenance wording at all, so CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE cannot catch them ('most adults need roughly 7-9 hours', 'light exposure is one input to the body's circadian timing system', 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness'), plus a logical non-sequitur reasoning backward from a metaphor's usefulness to a fact about the thing it describes ('if a single recovery night fully erased all sleep debt, the metaphor wouldn't be useful'), plus a bottom line that broke back into sleep/parenting/finance guidance and invented personal context nobody supplied in what_would_change_the_answer. FIX (prompt-level, not regex — this class of error has no stable lexical marker a regex can key on): new rule 27 ('WHAT AUTHORIZES THIS SENTENCE?') gives the model an explicit 3-way test before writing any factual sentence — A. USER_CLAIM (the visitor supplied it), B. LOGIC (follows from the claim's own structure, no empirical finding needed), C. LABELED_BACKGROUND (genuinely ordinary vocabulary-only background, used sparingly, never the central empirical answer) — rewrite or remove if none apply. New rule 28 fixes the metaphor non-sequitur (critique what a metaphor fails to establish, never reason backward from 'what would make it useful'). New rule 29 locks the bottom line to summarizing the claim analysis only, and reserves personal-situation language in what_would_change_the_answer for when the visitor actually supplied enough personal context to identify a real gap. NORTH STAR gained a prepended 3-line frame: use knowledge to understand the claim, logic to test it, evidence to settle it. TRAP HIT AND FIXED DURING THIS PASS: the rule 27/29 illustrative BAD examples quoted the exact attractor phrase 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness' TWICE, verbatim — live testing showed the model echoing that near-verbatim phrase straight into output (a known trap: worked BAD-example text gets copied rather than avoided, see deftbrain-voice-prompt-traps memory). Fixed by rewriting both examples to describe the ERROR PATTERN in the abstract (no specific number, no specific mechanism, no specific magnitude-of-benefit claim to copy) plus an explicit 'this is illustrating a pattern, not a script — a close paraphrase is the same violation' instruction. Verified 0 banned-phrase / 0 attractor-phrase hits across 3 consecutive live regenerations of the exact sleep scenario after the reword (the run before the reword produced the attractor phrase; the runs after did not). UI: added a visible 'No outside sources reviewed' sub-label beside the CLAIM ANALYSIS badge (the existing badge only had it in a hover tooltip, poor discoverability) and a 'Research These Claims' disclosure at the end of results, built from still_worth_verifying (falling back to what_would_change_the_answer) with one external search-engine link per open question — pure frontend, no new backend capability. This is deliberately NOT a live-retrieval / verified-research mode: the tool has no wired search or fetch capability, and building real retrieval is an infrastructure decision (external dependency, cost per request, latency, reliability) flagged to the owner rather than silently built or silently dropped, same position as the v5 note. i18n: svn_honest_uncertainty relabeled '? What Could Change the Answer' -> '? What Would Help' across all 13 languages (claim-analysis mode is never about the visitor's personal situation, so the more evidence-focused label is now the default; a personalized 'what could change the answer' framing would need a genuinely supplied personal-context case, which this tool does not yet branch on). New keys: svn_no_sources_reviewed, svn_research_these_claims, svn_research_intro, svn_search_this (13 languages each). DO NOT re-quote a specific number, mechanism, or magnitude figure in rule 27/28/29's illustrative examples — describe the pattern, never the sentence.
_meta.v7_note: V7 replaces 'regex + one regen' with a five-stage CLAIM ANALYSIS VALIDATION PIPELINE in the route: (1) CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, demoted to cheap first-pass detection; (2) a SEMANTIC EMPIRICAL-RESOLUTION CHECK — a judged call asking ONE narrow question per field (does this text assert or rely on a real-world proposition that was not supplied, not sourced in this run, and materially helps decide the claim? hedges do not convert FAIL to PASS); (3) one per-field REWRITE with the owner's exact rewrite prompt; (4) REVALIDATE the rewrite alone (regex + judge, batch size 1); (5) a fixed, LOCALIZED SAFE FALLBACK per field type (13 languages, in CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS) — never a second regeneration, because a validator/regenerator loop is exactly how the model finds new vocabulary for the same assertion. Fields with no fallback (a signal item's claim, a still_worth_verifying question, a sources_of_noise field, a person-specific item) are blanked so the structural filter drops the item. 5b: a signal item whose basis fell back gets its CLAIM re-judged alone and dropped unless it passes — a fixed basis under an unlicensed claim would lend it the very logical veneer the pipeline removes. WHY: five consecutive prompt-only passes (tool rules 14/27-29, then two rounds of the global epistemics contract) all failed the same live nutrition test the same way — the model stopped saying 'research shows' and started stating bare or hedged premises ('hormones regulate appetite and energy expenditure', 'meal timing may interact with circadian rhythms', 'intermittent fasting is a workable structure for some people'), or laundering them through 'this follows from the accounting relationship'. No lexical marker exists for that; a phrase list structurally cannot see it. MEASURED DURING BUILD: (a) judge recall collapses with batch size — one call over all 48 fields flagged 3 and missed the two plainest violations; the same two fields alone were both flagged in 1.7s — hence SEMANTIC_BATCH_SIZE=6, parallel; (b) the judge is consistent (3/3) on what it flags but neighborhood-sensitive, hence two offset passes unioned at stage 2; (c) the judge itself got laundered by 'this follows from the structure...' framing until told to judge every sentence on its own. Standalone replay of a leaked response through the finished pipeline: semantic=9 rewritten=6 fallback=2 blanked=1, and a fresh judge pass over the result found the flagship leaks gone. Live: 4 consecutive runs, fallbacks firing 1-5 times per run, route time ~60s (parallel judge calls; +10-20s vs v6). COST: roughly 20-35 small MODELS.SMART calls per request on a leaky response — a deliberate trade for a tool whose entire promise is this discipline. GOLDEN: schema unchanged; sources_of_noise and what_general_claims_cant_decide are now optionalSections on every case because the pipeline legitimately empties them (their fields have no fallback text, so a flagged item drops). DO NOT: collapse the judge back to one big batch; add a second regeneration attempt; let a rewrite through when its recheck was unavailable; give sources_of_noise/still_worth_verifying fields a fallback (they'd become filler).
_meta.v7_1_note: V7.1 (same day): SEMANTIC_CHECK_SYSTEM is now the owner's supplied validation prompt (PASS only if every substantive claim is visitor-supplied or logical analysis needing no extra real-world premise; FAIL on remembered knowledge, unsupplied examples, 'unestablished then asserted anyway', hedge-disguised claims, conclusions not established by validated material; counterfactual key test), wrapped in the batch/JSON contract plus a CLARIFICATIONS block. Measured: as written it over-flagged the tool's own correct output (flagged 'is an empirical question this analysis cannot settle'; one live run blanked the whole Signal section). Restoring the owner's earlier 'ignore statements that merely define / analyze wording / identify missing info / say evidence is needed' list fixed that (replay: blanked 1 -> 0, signal item kept). Live cost with the final prompt on the nutrition scenario: 12 fallbacks in one run (5/8 bottom-line items boilerplate) — the rule applied faithfully; boilerplate density is the owner's call, documented in the tool notes. Flagship BAD sentences ('hormonal factors operate within the energy-balance relationship', 'not competing explanations — they interact') added verbatim to MUST-fail examples after the solo re-judge passed one of them once.
_meta.v7_2_note: V7.2 (same day): fallback PRESENTATION only, judge untouched. (1) bottom_line fallback split into per-list wording takeaway/skeptical/would_help, each with a _many variant, 13 languages. (2) optional sub-fields (kernel_of_truth, signal limits) are OMITTED on failure (null) instead of replaced — UI renders them only when present. (3) collapseBottomLineFallbacks: within each bottom-line list, survivors untouched, all fallback items fold into at most one bullet placed last (singular wording for one failure, _many for several) — a variable-length Bottom Line, per DEFTBRAIN_OUTPUT_STANDARD_V2's preference for omission over redundant completeness. Bug caught by the fallback unit test before shipping: English would_help fallbacks began 'Evidence about…', matching CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, so the structural filter would have dropped the collapsed bullet; reworded. Live run 7: one collapsed takeaway bullet, kernels 3/4 (one omitted), no repeated fallbacks.
_meta.v8_note: V8 (2026-09-11): owner-supplied rebuild replaces the source-free claim-analysis architecture (V4-V7.2) with research-first: lib/claimResearch.js runs a bounded Anthropic web_search pre-pass through groundedFacts (maxUses default 6 for this tool, 3 everywhere else), returns a structured evidence packet, and the synthesis call (no tools) may make empirical claims ONLY from the packet with source_ids validated in code. New response fields: analysis_mode='verified_research', research_status, researched_at, sources_examined[{id,title,publisher,url,date,source_type}] (pruned to sources actually cited), and source_ids[] on the_signal items / the_noise items / still_worth_verifying items. Cold cache: waits up to SIGNAL_RESEARCH_COLD_WAIT_MS then returns HTTP 503 code:research_unavailable rather than an unresearched answer — so a golden re-run can 503 on a cold server; run the case once to warm (24h TTL), then check. the_noise is now optional (items without a surviving source id drop). The regex/judge/rewrite/fallback machinery and CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS are gone; earlier DO-NOT notes in SIGNALVSNOISE-NOTES.md V4-V7.2 are superseded, not reversed. See the V8 section there for kit findings.
_meta.v8_3_note: V8.3 (2026-09-11): speed. (1) synthesis split into two parallel disjoint-key calls (signal+noise 3000 tok / verify+cant-decide+bottom-line+sources-of-noise 2200 tok) — same packet, different schema halves; (2) hard word caps per field in the prompt; (3) two-phase UX: new POST /signal-vs-noise/research returns immediately ({status:'pending', sources:[]} 202 while the fetch runs, {status:'ready', researched_at, claim_count, sources} once cached — starts the fetch on a cold topic; own rate-limit bucket 20/min), the client polls it every ~6s untracked (pollToolEndpoint), shows 'N sources found', then calls the main endpoint which finds the research cached and runs synthesis only. Main endpoint unchanged for direct callers (60s cold wait, 503). New golden case research-status-investing-warm checks the readiness shape; sources optional because a cold server answers pending.

input.conflictingAdvice: Index funds always win vs. active management can beat the market, time in market beats timing the market vs. valuations matter, real estate vs. stocks

still_worth_verifying.question: Whether CAPE-based valuation signals provide actionable guidance beyond a 10-year forecasting horizon
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The 'valuations matter' claim implies strategic action, but the packet distinguishes forecasting power from profitable timing
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Primary research on whether portfolio adjustments triggered by CAPE levels improve net investor outcomes; only secondary sources found here

still_worth_verifying.question: Whether active management in less-efficient segments reliably outperforms net of fees over long horizons
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The packet notes small-cap and emerging markets may offer more opportunity, but 10-15 year underperformance rates still converge toward 75-85%
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Fee-adjusted, survivorship-controlled long-run data specific to small-cap and emerging-market active funds

still_worth_verifying.question: Whether real estate or stocks produce better returns once leverage, taxes, and management costs are fully accounted for in a specific jurisdiction
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The packet's headline return figures are unlevered and pre-tax; the comparison flips materially depending on how those factors are applied
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: After-tax, after-cost return data matched to the investor's jurisdiction and use of leverage; only secondary sources found here

still_worth_verifying.question: Whether the historical U.S. rolling-return record extends reliably to non-U.S. markets or future periods
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: 'Time in market' evidence rests heavily on U.S. equity history, which the packet itself flags as unusually favorable
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Long-run rolling-return data across multiple developed and emerging markets; only secondary sources found here

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether your specific investment horizon is long enough for 'time in market' to reliably protect you — the packet's rolling-return evidence covers 20-year windows, not shorter ones
Whether your tax situation, access to mortgage financing, and local property market make real estate or stocks more advantageous for you personally
Whether your ability to stay invested through sharp drawdowns makes the 'time in market' case relevant — behavioral capacity to hold is not something general evidence can assess for an individual

supported_takeaways: Most active large-cap funds underperform their benchmarks over long periods — 79% in 2025 alone, with persistent outperformers falling below chance rates — making low-cost index exposure hard to dismiss (S1, S3, S4)

High starting valuations as measured by CAPE have historically been associated with lower returns over the following decade, but this is a 10-year headwind signal, not a timing tool or crash predictor (S8, S9, S10)

Over 145 years across 16 countries, unlevered real estate and stock returns were comparable, but stocks decisively outperformed in the 1980-2015 sub-period; leverage, taxes, and costs shift the comparison significantly and individually (S11, S12)
treat_skeptically: 'Index funds always win' — the evidence shows a strong long-run tendency, not a universal law; short periods and some market segments have produced active outperformance (S1, S4)
Real estate vs. stocks framed as a clean contest — the packet shows the answer depends heavily on leverage, jurisdiction, time period, and cost assumptions that vary by person (S11, S12)
'Valuations matter' read as a signal to exit or wait — the packet explicitly finds CAPE does not support profitable market timing in practice (S9)
what_would_change_the_answer: Fee-adjusted, after-tax return comparisons for the investor's specific jurisdiction would materially shift the real estate vs. stocks conclusion
Evidence on whether CAPE-triggered allocation changes improve net outcomes for investors would determine whether 'valuations matter' is actionable or merely descriptive

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A strong central tendency ('most funds underperform') becomes an ironclad rule ('always'), hiding the variation that matters for specific decisions
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Any investing claim using 'always,' 'never,' or 'always wins'

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Headline return figures for real estate vs. stocks drop leverage, taxes, and transaction costs, making the comparison look simpler than it is
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Return comparisons that do not specify levered vs. unlevered, pre- vs. after-tax, or gross vs. net of costs

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A 10-year return predictor like CAPE gets presented as a reason to act now, collapsing a decade-horizon signal into a near-term call
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Arguments that high valuations mean 'the market will fall soon' rather than 'expected returns are lower over the next decade'

output.topic_as_understood: Whether index funds reliably beat active management, whether staying invested matters more than timing, whether valuations predict returns, and how real estate compares to stocks over the long run
output.framing: Most of these conflicts dissolve when you separate time horizon from trading horizon, and tendency from absolute rule — the evidence supports strong tendencies with real exceptions, not universal laws.

items.claim: Most active large-cap equity funds underperform their benchmark over time, and consistent outperformance is rarer than chance alone would predict.
items.basis: S&P Dow Jones Indices SPIVA scorecards — covering 25 years of U.S. fund data using a survivorship-bias-controlled database — found 79% of active large-cap funds underperformed the S&P 500 in 2025, and only 4.5% of above-median funds stayed above median persistently, below the 6.25% rate expected from random chance. Underperformance also appeared across 11 international regions.
items.limits: SPIVA tracks mutual funds; hedge funds and institutional separately managed accounts are not fully captured. Some less-efficient segments — certain small-cap and emerging market categories — have shown more active opportunity, though long-horizon underperformance rates still converge toward 75–85% even there.

the_noise.claim: Index funds always beat active management
the_noise.noise_label: Strong tendency stated as universal law
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Over most long horizons and in most market segments, most active funds underperform their benchmark after costs — but not universally, and specific segments and short periods have produced active outperformance.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The word 'always' claims a universal law; the evidence supports a strong long-run central tendency with documented exceptions across segments, years, and fund structures.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: The long-run odds heavily favor index funds for most investors in most mainstream equity categories.

the_noise.claim: Time in the market beats timing the market vs. valuations matter — framed as contradictory
the_noise.noise_label: Two claims about different things treated as opposites
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: The CAPE ratio research addresses 10-year return forecasting, not short-run trading signals. 'Stay invested' advice addresses the cost of exiting and missing recovery days. The research packet treats these as separate questions operating on different horizons.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Pitting these against each other implies they answer the same question. The packet notes that high CAPE predicts lower average returns over the following decade but does not provide actionable timing information — so both ideas can be true simultaneously without contradiction.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Starting valuations do carry information about long-run expected returns, even when they cannot tell you when to trade.

the_noise.claim: Real estate vs. stocks — one clearly wins
the_noise.noise_label: Single-winner framing for a context-dependent comparison
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Over 145 years across 16 countries, unlevered inflation-adjusted returns were comparable (roughly 7% real for residential real estate, 6.9% for equities), but stocks decisively outpaced real estate in the 1980–2015 sub-period. Leverage, taxes, geography, and income reinvestment all shift the comparison materially.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Declaring a winner ignores that the answer changes depending on time period, whether leverage is included, local market, tax treatment, and whether rental income is reinvested — all of which the evidence identifies as critical variables.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Both asset classes have produced meaningful long-run real returns; their risk profiles and liquidity differ substantially, which matters as much as raw return figures.

input.conflictingAdvice: Indexfonds gewinnen immer vs. aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen, Zeit im Markt schlaegt Markt-Timing vs. Bewertungen sind wichtig

still_worth_verifying.question: Wie stark gilt die SPIVA-Underperformance-Tendenz für aktiv verwaltete Fonds in Deutschland und Europa?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Die SPIVA-Daten beziehen sich auf US-Märkte; ob deutsche Anleger ähnliche Ergebnisse erwarten können, ist im Paket nicht belegt.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Eine vergleichbare europäische Persistenz-Scorecard oder Peer-reviewed-Studie zu aktiv verwalteten Fonds in Deutschland

still_worth_verifying.question: Gilt die mathematisch belegte Asymmetrie von Market-Timing-Renditen auch für nicht-US-Märkte und kürzere Anlagehorizonte?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Die Studie nutzt US-Daten; für deutsche Anleger mit kürzerem Horizont ist die Übertragbarkeit offen.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Replikationsstudien für europäische Indizes über verschiedene Zeitfenster

still_worth_verifying.question: Verändert die gestiegene Dominanz weniger Megacap-Aktien die historische Erklärungskraft des CAPE für künftige Renditen?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Wenn CAPE durch Marktstrukturveränderungen verzerrt ist, sind Renditeerwartungen auf Basis historischer CAPE-Werte weniger zuverlässig.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Neuere Studien, die Marktkonzentration als Störvariable in CAPE-Prognosemodellen berücksichtigen

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Ob ein bestimmter aktiv verwalteter Fonds, den der Anleger konkret in Betracht zieht, zu den wenigen langfristigen Outperformern gehören wird – das lässt sich aus den allgemeinen Daten nicht ableiten.
Ob der individuelle Anlagehorizont, die Risikobereitschaft und der geplante Zeitpunkt von Einzahlungen dafür sorgen, dass Bewertungssignale (CAPE) praktisch relevant werden oder nicht.

Ob eine bewertungsbasierte Anpassung der Aktienquote für diesen Anleger eine bessere Erwartungsrendite erzeugt als ein striktes Buy-and-Hold – das hängt von Zeitpunkt, Kosten und Umsetzung ab, die das Paket nicht beantwortet.

supported_takeaways: Über lange Zeiträume haben rund 79 % der aktiven US-Large-Cap-Fonds den S&P 500 nicht geschlagen; vergangene Outperformance sagt künftige Outperformance kaum voraus. [S1]
Die Wahrscheinlichkeitsverteilung von Market-Timing-Renditen ist asymmetrisch zugunsten unterdurchschnittlicher Ergebnisse – selbst vor Transaktionskosten. [S6]
Hohe Bewertungen (gemessen am P/E bzw. CAPE) sind mit niedrigeren erwarteten Renditen über 10+ Jahre verbunden, liefern aber kein verlässliches kurzfristiges Einstiegssignal. [S11, S12]
treat_skeptically: 'Indexfonds gewinnen immer' – das Wort 'immer' ist nicht gedeckt: In einzelnen Jahren, Kategorien und kurzen Zeitfenstern schlägt eine Minderheit aktiver Fonds den Index. [S1]
Aktives Management pauschal als marktschlagend darstellen – Persistenzdaten deuten eher auf Zufall als auf reproduzierbares Können hin. [S1]
Bewertungen als Timing-Werkzeug nutzen – CAPE erklärt langfristige Renditeerwartungen, nicht den Zeitpunkt der nächsten Korrektur. [S11, S12]
what_would_change_the_answer: Belastbare europäische oder deutsche Daten zur Aktivfonds-Underperformance könnten die US-basierten SPIVA-Befunde relativieren oder bestätigen.

Studien, die bewertungsbasierte taktische Allokation (kein reines kurzfristiges Timing) über lange Zeiträume und verschiedene Märkte untersuchen, würden die offene Frage zur Verbindung von Bewertung und Handlung beantworten.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Eine starke Mehrheitstendenz ('79 % schlechter') wird zur universellen Regel ('immer'), obwohl Ausnahmen dokumentiert sind.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Fehlende Zeitangaben und Kategorisierungen bei Renditebehauptungen

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Geschlossene oder fusionierte Fonds fallen aus Statistiken heraus, wodurch aktive Fonds besser erscheinen als sie im Durchschnitt waren.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Vergleiche ohne Hinweis darauf, ob aufgelöste Fonds einbezogen wurden

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Langfristige Renditeprognosen durch Bewertungsmaße werden als kurzfristige Kauf- oder Verkaufssignale umgedeutet.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Empfehlungen, jetzt aus- oder einzusteigen, die sich allein auf CAPE oder P/E berufen

output.topic_as_understood: Welche Anlagestrategie ist besser: passive Indexfonds, aktives Management oder bewertungsbasiertes Timing?
output.framing: Die drei Aussagen betreffen unterschiedliche Zeiträume und Fragen – Kosten und Persistenz (aktiv vs. passiv), Einstiegszeitpunkt (Timing) und langfristige Renditeerwartung (Bewertung) – und widersprechen sich weniger, als es scheint.

items.claim: Die Mehrheit aktiv verwalteter Large-Cap-Fonds bleibt langfristig hinter dem Index zurück.
items.basis: Die SPIVA-Datenbank von S&P Dow Jones Indices – ein offizieller Datensatz mit Korrektur für Survivorship Bias – zeigt, dass über 25 Jahre rund 79 % der aktiven US-Large-Cap-Fonds den S&P 500 verfehlten.
items.limits: Die Daten beziehen sich auf den US-Markt; ob deutsche oder europäische Fonds ähnlich abschneiden, ist durch das vorliegende Paket nicht direkt belegt.

items.claim: Vergangene Outperformance eines aktiven Fonds sagt künftige Outperformance nicht verlässlich vorher.
items.basis: Die SPIVA Persistence Scorecard zeigt, dass die Zahlen bei Large-Cap-Fonds eher auf Zufall als auf Können hindeuten – ein Manager, der zuletzt besser war, bietet keine verlässliche Grundlage für die Auswahl.
items.limits: Kurzfristige Phasen relativer Stärke existieren; im ersten Halbjahr 2025 lagen nur 54 % der Aktivfonds unter der Benchmark.

items.claim: Dauerhaft investiert bleiben schlägt kurzfristiges Markt-Timing wahrscheinlich – schon vor Transaktionskosten.
items.basis: Eine mathematische Analyse in einer peer-reviewed Fachzeitschrift zeigt, dass die Renditeverteilung von Market-Timing asymmetrisch ist: Das wahrscheinlichste Ergebnis liegt unter der Marktrendite.
items.limits: Die Analyse basiert auf US-Marktdaten; ob die gleiche Asymmetrie in allen Märkten und kürzeren Zeitfenstern gilt, ist nicht abschließend belegt.

items.claim: Hohe Bewertungen (z. B. hohes CAPE) sind mit niedrigeren langfristigen Renditeerwartungen verbunden – aber kein Timing-Signal.
items.basis: Campbell und Shiller zeigten, dass P/E-Ratios die Renditen über 10+ Jahre erklären, nicht über ein Jahr. Eine Analyse von 17 MSCI-Länderindizes bestätigte diesen Zusammenhang länderübergreifend.
items.limits: Ein hohes CAPE schließt weitere Kursgewinne auf Jahre nicht aus und liefert kein verlässliches Signal, wann eine Korrektur einsetzt.

the_noise.noise_label: Absoluter Anspruch, den die Daten nicht stützen
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Die Mehrheit aktiver Large-Cap-Fonds bleibt langfristig hinter dem Index zurück – nicht alle, nicht in jedem Jahr und nicht in jeder Kategorie.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: 'Immer' schließt Ausnahmen aus, die SPIVA ausdrücklich dokumentiert: Einzeljahre, bestimmte Kategorien und kurze Zeitfenster, in denen eine Minderheit aktiver Fonds besser abschneidet.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Über lange Zeiträume und nach Kosten ist die Mehrheit aktiver Fonds im Nachteil.

the_noise.claim: Aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen (als allgemeine Handlungsempfehlung).
the_noise.noise_label: Möglich, aber ex ante nicht verlässlich identifizierbar
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Einige aktive Fonds übertreffen in bestimmten Zeiträumen den Markt, doch vergangene Outperformance sagt künftige nicht zuverlässig voraus.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Die Aussage ist technisch wahr, aber ohne Hinweis auf Persistenz und Kosten irreführend: Wer den künftigen Gewinner ex ante erkennt, ist die offene – und laut SPIVA ungelöste – Frage.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Kurzfristige Phasen, in denen die Mehrheit der Aktivfonds besser abschneidet, kommen vor.

the_noise.claim: Bewertungen sind wichtig (implizit: als Timing-Werkzeug für Kauf- und Verkaufsentscheidungen).
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Bewertungskennzahlen wie CAPE erklären langfristige Renditeerwartungen über 10+ Jahre, liefern aber kein verlässliches Signal für kurzfristige Ein- oder Ausstiegszeitpunkte.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Die belegte Erklärungskraft gilt für den 10-Jahres-Horizont. Wer daraus ableitet, jetzt kaufen oder verkaufen zu sollen, überträgt ein langfristiges Prognosewerkzeug auf eine Frage, für die es nicht konstruiert wurde.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Hohe Bewertungen senken die zu erwartende langfristige Rendite – dieser Zusammenhang ist länderübergreifend belegt.

input.conflictingAdvice: Screen time is destroying kids vs. it depends on content, tiger parenting vs. free-range, homework helps vs. homework is harmful

still_worth_verifying.question: Does content type and parental co-viewing meaningfully change screen time outcomes, independent of total duration?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Most studies measure total time, not content — so the 'it depends on content' claim has limited direct empirical support despite being plausible.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Studies that experimentally vary content type and co-viewing while holding duration constant, especially for under-fives.

still_worth_verifying.question: Do tiger parenting findings from Asian-American and Hong Kong samples apply to other cultural or demographic groups?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The visitor's claim frames tiger vs. free-range as a general parenting debate, but the research base is concentrated in specific cultural contexts.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Longitudinal studies of tiger parenting across diverse cultural populations using consistent construct definitions.

still_worth_verifying.question: At what homework volume do benefits plateau or reverse, and does this differ meaningfully by subject or student circumstances?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The 'homework is harmful' claim likely rests on excess-homework concerns, but the packet notes thresholds are debated rather than established.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Experimental or quasi-experimental studies that vary homework quantity systematically across grade levels and subjects.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether a specific child's screen use is harmful, given that outcomes vary by content, duration, context, and individual developmental factors that general studies do not capture.

Whether a particular family's stricter or more permissive parenting approach will help or harm their child, since cultural fit, family warmth, and child temperament are not addressed by the group-level research.

Whether a specific child should do more or less homework, since grade level, subject, homework quality, and home resources all moderate benefit in ways a general evidence summary cannot resolve for one student.

supported_takeaways: Screen time harms are not uniform: the packet finds strongest negative associations with high volumes of passive and social media use; educational or co-viewed content shows weaker or inconsistent negative associations. [S3, S5, S6]

Homework benefit is heavily grade-dependent: near-zero association with achievement for young elementary students, rising substantially by high school — so 'homework helps' and 'homework is harmful' can both be partially correct depending on the child's age. [S10, S11]

Tiger parenting is associated with higher depressive symptoms and anxiety in the samples studied, while supportive parenting — high warmth, lower negativity — was linked to better outcomes in the same research. [S7, S8]
treat_skeptically: 'Screen time is destroying kids' — overstated as a universal; harm evidence is concentrated in high-volume passive use and social media, not all screen use. [S3, S5]
'Tiger parenting produces better outcomes' — the available evidence runs in the opposite direction for wellbeing in the populations studied. [S7, S8]
'Homework helps' as a general claim — not well-supported for elementary-age children, where the effect is near zero across multiple meta-analyses. [S10, S11]
what_would_change_the_answer: Causal evidence on screen time — current studies are predominantly observational, leaving reverse causation unresolved. [S1, S2, S4]
Research on tiger and free-range parenting in diverse cultural contexts, since current tiger parenting findings come from a narrow demographic range. [S7, S9]

sources_of_noise.source_type: Collapsing a variable into a single measure
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Treating all screen time as one thing obscures meaningful differences between content types, durations, and contexts — making moderate or qualified findings sound like blanket condemnations.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A claim says 'screen time' without specifying content, duration, or age group.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Results from one cultural or demographic sample get stated as general parenting truths, dropping the population limits the researchers themselves noted.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Parenting advice that cites a study but omits which group was studied, or applies findings across cultures without acknowledgment.

sources_of_noise.source_type: Omitting the grade-level moderator from homework claims
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Both 'homework helps' and 'homework is harmful' can be stated confidently by selecting evidence from different grade levels — the moderating variable disappears in popular summaries.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A homework claim that does not specify the age group or grade level it applies to.

output.topic_as_understood: Whether screen time universally harms children, whether tiger parenting outperforms other styles, and whether homework helps or hurts academic achievement
output.framing: Each claim treats a variable as fixed when the research consistently shows the outcome depends heavily on type, amount, age, and context — collapsing those distinctions is where most of the conflict comes from.

items.claim: Heavy passive screen use associates with poorer developmental outcomes, but the effect varies substantially by content type, duration, and whether a parent is co-viewing
items.basis: A 2026 systematic review of 46 studies and a 2025 UK government review of 48 systematic reviews both found that simple total-screen-time measures associate with developmental and health reductions, while educational or co-viewed content showed weaker or inconsistent negative associations. A 2025 JAMA cohort study (n=3,322 grade-3 children) linked higher total screen time to lower reading and math scores.
items.limits: Most studies are observational; reverse causation has not been ruled out, and the evidence base for children under 3 is comparatively thin with high risk of bias.

items.claim: Homework's benefit on academic achievement is strongly moderated by grade level: near zero for elementary students, modest for middle school, and meaningful for high school
items.basis: The Cooper, Robinson, and Patall (2006) meta-analysis — the most comprehensive synthesis of homework research — found correlations near zero at elementary level, approximately r=.07 at middle grades, and r=.25 at high school. A 2017 meta-analysis found similar effect-size gradients (roughly d≈0.15, 0.25, and 0.48 respectively).
items.limits: Most homework research is correlational; students who do more homework may already differ in motivation and resources, introducing confounding.

items.claim: Among Asian-American families studied, supportive parenting — not tiger parenting — was associated with the best academic outcomes; tiger parenting was linked to higher depressive symptoms and feelings of parental alienation
items.basis: A longitudinal study of over 400 Asian-American families found supportive parenting produced the highest GPAs, while children of tiger parents reported more depression and academic pressure. A 2018 primary study of 439 Hong Kong children linked child-perceived tiger parenting to significantly higher child anxiety.
items.limits: Research is concentrated in East Asian and Asian-American samples; generalizability to other cultural contexts is unclear, and tiger parenting is not standardized consistently across studies.

the_noise.noise_label: Collapses all screen use into one verdict
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: High volumes of passive entertainment screen use and social media — particularly for young girls — associate with worse outcomes; educational or co-viewed content shows weaker or inconsistent negative associations.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim treats all screen time as equivalent and all harm as certain, when multiple systematic reviews show effects depend heavily on content type, duration, and context.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: High total screen time, especially passive TV and social media, does associate with developmental and academic disadvantages across multiple large reviews.

the_noise.claim: Tiger parenting produces better child outcomes
the_noise.noise_label: Selects the achievement metric, ignores wellbeing data
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: In studied Asian-American samples, tiger parenting does not produce the best academic outcomes; supportive parenting does, while tiger parenting is associated with higher anxiety and depressive symptoms.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim focuses on achievement potential while the available longitudinal and primary research finds supportive parenting outperforms tiger parenting even on grades, and tiger parenting carries measurable wellbeing costs.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Tiger parenting is not purely authoritarian — it combines strictness with warmth — which may partially explain why some children of tiger parents perform reasonably academically despite elevated stress.

the_noise.claim: Homework helps (as a general claim across all children)
the_noise.noise_label: Ignores the grade-level finding that flips the conclusion
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Homework associates with meaningful achievement gains for high schoolers; for elementary students, the correlation is near zero across the most comprehensive meta-analyses — making a blanket 'homework helps' claim poorly supported.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Treating homework benefit as uniform ignores one of the most replicated moderating findings in this literature: age group changes the conclusion substantially.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: For middle and high school students, homework does associate with higher achievement across multiple meta-analyses, and e-homework shows a positive overall effect in a 2026 meta-analysis of 26 studies.

input.topic: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
input.conflictingAdvice: My coworker says blue light glasses fixed her insomnia. Another friend says sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends, but my doctor said catching up on weekends helps.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does blocking blue light via glasses produce a clinically meaningful subjective benefit even when objective actigraphy measures show no significant effect?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The coworker reports real improvement; the 2025 meta-analysis found non-significant objective results but could not rule out a genuine effect given only 49 participants.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Larger RCTs separating subjective sleep quality from actigraphy outcomes, and distinguishing insomnia subtypes from general poor sleepers.

still_worth_verifying.question: How much does the severity and duration of sleep restriction determine whether weekend catch-up sleep restores cognitive and metabolic function?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Your doctor and friend disagree; the packet suggests both positions have partial support, but recovery likely depends on how deep the debt is.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Controlled trials distinguishing acute sleep loss from chronic restriction, with pre-specified metabolic and cognitive endpoints.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does the circadian disruption from irregular weekend sleep timing cancel out the benefit of extra hours for a given individual?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: If social jet lag outweighs recovery benefit, the doctor's advice could backfire depending on how far the person shifts their schedule.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Studies tracking both total sleep hours and sleep-timing shift together with health outcomes in the same individuals over time.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether the coworker's insomnia improvement from blue light glasses reflects a real effect, a placebo effect, or an improvement in her specific context — her individual report cannot be resolved by population-level RCT averages.
What your personal sleep need is — the packet establishes a healthy adult range of roughly 7–9 hours, not a single number, and individual variation is real but not measurable from general evidence.

Whether weekend catch-up sleep helps or harms you specifically depends on how restricted your weekday sleep is, how much your timing shifts, and your metabolic baseline — none of which the general evidence can supply.

supported_takeaways: The healthy adult sleep range supported by major professional bodies is 7–9 hours, not a fixed 8; both genuine short sleep and long sleep associate with worse health outcomes in population data. [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5]

Weekend catch-up sleep offers partial recovery — some mood, fatigue, and cognitive benefit — but the packet also associates irregular sleep timing with circadian and metabolic costs; both your friend and your doctor have partial support. [S8, S9, S10]

Blue light glasses show conflicting results across a 2025 meta-analysis (no significant objective effect, n=49) and an earlier systematic review (benefit in sleep-disordered populations); the evidence is mixed and the sample sizes too small to settle it. [S6, S7]
treat_skeptically: 'Fixed 8 hours' framing — professional bodies recommend a range; the single-number claim is overstated. [S1, S2, S3]
'Blue light glasses fixed her insomnia' as a general claim — one person's outcome cannot be read from small, conflicting trials with non-significant objective results. [S6, S7]
Either absolute position on weekend catch-up — 'fully repays debt' or 'never helps' — goes beyond what the mixed observational and review evidence supports. [S8, S9, S10]
what_would_change_the_answer: Larger, adequately powered RCTs on blue light glasses with both subjective and objective endpoints would clarify whether the effect is real or an artifact of small samples.
Controlled studies tracking sleep-timing shift alongside extra hours during weekend recovery would show whether circadian disruption or added sleep duration dominates the health outcome.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A headline-friendly figure like '8 hours' gets repeated until it displaces the actual recommended range of 7–9 hours.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim uses one number where guidelines specify a range.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A plausible biological mechanism plus one person's improvement makes a product sound proven even when trials show non-significant effects.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The explanation of why it works is offered as evidence that it does work.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Mixed evidence — catch-up sleep helps somewhat but also carries circadian costs — gets compressed into 'you can' or 'you cannot' repay sleep debt.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim admits no conditions, degree, or tradeoff where the opposite might also be partly true.

output.topic_as_understood: Whether sleep need is fixed at 8 hours, whether blue-light blocking glasses treat insomnia, and whether weekend sleep can repay sleep debt
output.framing: All three claims collapse a real but nuanced finding into a single rule. The evidence supports ranges and partial effects, not absolutes.

items.claim: Adults have a healthy sleep range of roughly 7-9 hours, not a fixed 8-hour requirement
items.basis: The CDC, AASM, Sleep Research Society, American Heart Association, and National Sleep Foundation all recommend 7 or more hours rather than a fixed 8. Cross-sectional data associate both short sleep (under 6 hours) and long sleep (9 or more hours) with worse cardiovascular outcomes compared to the 7-8 hour range.
items.limits: Individual need varies; some people may function adequately outside this range. Association data cannot confirm sleep duration itself causes harm.

items.claim: Weekend catch-up sleep offers partial recovery but does not fully reverse chronic sleep debt, and may carry its own costs
items.basis: A 2025 systematic review found catch-up sleep partially restores mood and some cognitive function but cannot fully offset chronic deprivation. A separate 2025 study found that shifting sleep timing on weekends can disrupt circadian rhythms and impair metabolic regulation, partly offsetting the extra hours gained.
items.limits: Most supporting evidence is observational. How much recovery occurs depends on how severe and prolonged the sleep restriction was.

items.claim: Blue-light blocking glasses show mixed results: some benefit in certain populations, no significant objective effect on sleep in small RCTs
items.basis: A 2025 pre-registered meta-analysis of 3 double-blind crossover RCTs (49 participants total) found non-significant improvements in sleep onset, total sleep time, and efficiency on objective actigraphy measures. An earlier 2021 systematic review found evidence supporting reduced sleep onset latency in insomnia patients and shift workers.
items.limits: The RCT evidence base is very small (49 participants) and underpowered. Subjective benefit and objective benefit may differ, and placebo effects cannot be ruled out.

the_noise.claim: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
the_noise.noise_label: One number does not fit all
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Major health bodies recommend a 7-9 hour range for adults, with real health risks appearing mainly below 6 hours or above 9.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The wording fixes an imprecise population guideline into a single threshold and treats the range as universal law.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Short sleep is genuinely associated with increased depression risk and worse cardiovascular outcomes in population data.

the_noise.claim: Blue light glasses fixed her insomnia (implying they are an effective insomnia treatment)
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Objective RCT evidence (49 people, 3 trials) found no significant sleep improvements; some benefit in specific populations appears in earlier reviews. No clinical guidelines recommend them as a primary insomnia treatment.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: A personal positive experience is presented as proof of efficacy for insomnia broadly, when the controlled evidence is mixed and the sample sizes too small to settle the question.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Blue light does suppress melatonin via an established biological mechanism, and earlier reviews found some benefit in shift workers and insomnia patients.

the_noise.claim: Sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends at all (absolute version) OR catching up fully restores you (absolute version)
the_noise.noise_label: Both all-or-nothing positions miss the middle
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Catch-up sleep partially restores mood and some performance but does not fully reverse chronic deprivation, and irregular sleep timing may add circadian costs even while adding hours.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Both the friend and the doctor state one side of a genuinely mixed picture as if the evidence settles it cleanly.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Cross-sectional studies associate weekend catch-up sleep with lower depression, lower BMI, and reduced metabolic syndrome compared to staying sleep-deprived.
